His voice was muffled and his speech was dysarthric. He appeared lethargic but had no focal neurologic deficits. Physical examination findings were normal except for tonsillar edema. White blood cell count was 13.4 ×103/μL (reference, 4-11 ×103/μL); blood glucose level, 274 mg/dL (15.21 mmol/L) (reference, 70-100 mg/dL [3.89-5.55 mmol/L]); serum creatinine level, 0.9 mg/dL (79.56 μmol/L) (reference, 0.4-1.3 mg/dL [35.36-114.92 μmol/L]); bicarbonate level, 9 mmol/L (reference, 20-30 mmol/L); arterial pH, 7.21 (reference, 7.35-7.45); β-hydroxybutyric acid level, 58.2 mg/dL (5590 μmol/L) (reference, <2.81 mg/dL [269.9 μmol/L]); and serum anion gap, 21 (reference, 7-17). Findings on a chest radiograph were normal. A computed tomography scan of the head and neck with intravenous contrast showed mucosal thickening of the maxillary and ethmoid sinuses, and prominence of the adenoids and palatine tonsils. Flexible laryngoscopy showed patent nasal sinuses and mucosal edema without abscess or necrosis. He was treated with intravenous fluids and with insulin, vancomycin (1 g intravenously every 12 hours), and piperacillin-tazobactam (4.5 g intravenously every 6 hours). case_info.explanation: A. Initiate liposomal amphotericin B (5 mg/kg intravenously daily) The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that the nonseptate right-angled hyphae present in the sinus mucosal biopsy sample are diagnostic of mucormycosis. Obtaining a serum (1,3)-β-D-glucan level (choice B) would not be helpful because it detects a fungal cell wall component that is absent in mucormycetes. Fluconazole (choice C) is not recommended because it is inactive against fungi that cause mucormycosis. Steroids (choice D) are contraindicated because they may increase the invasiveness of nasopharyngeal mucormycosis. Mucormycosis is a disease caused by a heterogeneous group of more than 250 fungal species.Rhizopus,Mucor,Lichtheimia, andRhizomucorare the most frequent human pathogens1and are present worldwide.2Rhino-orbital-cerebral infection is the most common clinical presentation of mucormycosis, although other organs such as the lung, intestines, and skin can become infected.2,3Rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis typically enters the body through inhalation of spores that deposit in the nasopharynx or through penetrating trauma.2It is a rapidly progressive infection that can involve the brain and is associated with a mortality rate of 25% to 62%.2-4Patients at highest risk of rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis are those with poorly controlled diabetes, high serum iron levels (eg, hemochromatosis), and prolonged neutropenia or impaired cellular immunity (eg, hematologic malignancies; solid organ or bone marrow transplants).2,3SARS-CoV-2 infection is also associated with rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis, especially among patients treated with steroids who develop hyperglycemia.5National epidemiology studies are lacking, but 1 study estimated the annual incidence of mucormycosis at 3 cases/million individuals in the US.6 Patients with mucormycosis may present with orbital swelling, facial pain, proptosis, cranial nerve palsies, headache, acute vision loss, and, in severe cases, a facial necrotic eschar. Among immunosuppressed patients, the primary differential diagnosis is invasive fungal rhinosinusitis due toAspergillus. The diagnosis of mucormycosis is based on histopathology, which shows characteristic nonseptate right-angled hyphae often appearing in “ribbon formations,”3angioinvasion and infarction of surrounding tissue, and, rarely, fruiting bodies, the morphologically distinctive spore-producing component of the fungus. Staining and culture of tissues containing fungus7can help identify fungal species and identify antimicrobial susceptibility. Polymerase chain reaction testing of tissue specimens may be used to identify the specific fungus when histopathology is consistent with mucormycosis but a fungal culture result is negative.3,8 Patients with rhino-orbital-cerebral disease who have risk factors for mucormycosis (eg, uncontrolled diabetes, immunosuppression) need prompt evaluation and surgical debridement of all infected tissue. First-line treatment for rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis is liposomal amphotericin B, which should be administered promptly after diagnosis is suspected and is typically prescribed for 4 to 6 weeks, although duration of therapy depends on clinical improvement and the level of immunosuppression. Oral isavuconazole and posaconazole are less effective medications but may be used if liposomal amphotericin B is contraindicated; they may be coadministered with liposomal amphotericin B in patients with severe disease or may be prescribed as step-down therapy after improvement with liposomal amphotericin B.3 The patient was treated empirically with intravenous liposomal amphotericin B beginning intraoperatively. One week later, the result of an 18s rRNA gene-based polymerase chain reaction test performed on sinus mucosal biopsy tissue was positive for theRhizopus oryzaecomplex. Repeat fiberoptic laryngoscopy on postoperative day 1 revealed no residual necrotic tissue but identified new vocal cord paralysis, for which the patient underwent an elective tracheostomy and placement of a gastrostomy tube 2 days after his initial surgery. He underwent decannulation 2 months later and was discharged home after a 65-day hospitalization, during which he was treated with liposomal amphotericin B (5 mg/kg intravenously daily for 4 weeks) and then transitioned to oral posaconazole (delayed-release, 300 mg daily). At follow-up 1 week after discharge, he reported no significant concerns other than some difficulty with phonation. He was instructed to continue posaconazole for an additional 3 months.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: A. Initiate liposomal amphotericin B (5 mg/kg intravenously daily) The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that the nonseptate right-angled hyphae present in the sinus mucosal biopsy sample are diagnostic of mucormycosis. Obtaining a serum (1,3)-β-D-glucan level (choice B) would not be helpful because it detects a fungal cell wall component that is absent in mucormycetes. Fluconazole (choice C) is not recommended because it is inactive against fungi that cause mucormycosis. Steroids (choice D) are contraindicated because they may increase the invasiveness of nasopharyngeal mucormycosis. Mucormycosis is a disease caused by a heterogeneous group of more than 250 fungal species.Rhizopus,Mucor,Lichtheimia, andRhizomucorare the most frequent human pathogens1and are present worldwide.2Rhino-orbital-cerebral infection is the most common clinical presentation of mucormycosis, although other organs such as the lung, intestines, and skin can become infected.2,3Rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis typically enters the body through inhalation of spores that deposit in the nasopharynx or through penetrating trauma.2It is a rapidly progressive infection that can involve the brain and is associated with a mortality rate of 25% to 62%.2-4Patients at highest risk of rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis are those with poorly controlled diabetes, high serum iron levels (eg, hemochromatosis), and prolonged neutropenia or impaired cellular immunity (eg, hematologic malignancies; solid organ or bone marrow transplants).2,3SARS-CoV-2 infection is also associated with rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis, especially among patients treated with steroids who develop hyperglycemia.5National epidemiology studies are lacking, but 1 study estimated the annual incidence of mucormycosis at 3 cases/million individuals in the US.6 Patients with mucormycosis may present with orbital swelling, facial pain, proptosis, cranial nerve palsies, headache, acute vision loss, and, in severe cases, a facial necrotic eschar. Among immunosuppressed patients, the primary differential diagnosis is invasive fungal rhinosinusitis due toAspergillus. The diagnosis of mucormycosis is based on histopathology, which shows characteristic nonseptate right-angled hyphae often appearing in “ribbon formations,”3angioinvasion and infarction of surrounding tissue, and, rarely, fruiting bodies, the morphologically distinctive spore-producing component of the fungus. Staining and culture of tissues containing fungus7can help identify fungal species and identify antimicrobial susceptibility. Polymerase chain reaction testing of tissue specimens may be used to identify the specific fungus when histopathology is consistent with mucormycosis but a fungal culture result is negative.3,8 Patients with rhino-orbital-cerebral disease who have risk factors for mucormycosis (eg, uncontrolled diabetes, immunosuppression) need prompt evaluation and surgical debridement of all infected tissue. First-line treatment for rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis is liposomal amphotericin B, which should be administered promptly after diagnosis is suspected and is typically prescribed for 4 to 6 weeks, although duration of therapy depends on clinical improvement and the level of immunosuppression. Oral isavuconazole and posaconazole are less effective medications but may be used if liposomal amphotericin B is contraindicated; they may be coadministered with liposomal amphotericin B in patients with severe disease or may be prescribed as step-down therapy after improvement with liposomal amphotericin B.3 The patient was treated empirically with intravenous liposomal amphotericin B beginning intraoperatively. One week later, the result of an 18s rRNA gene-based polymerase chain reaction test performed on sinus mucosal biopsy tissue was positive for theRhizopus oryzaecomplex. Repeat fiberoptic laryngoscopy on postoperative day 1 revealed no residual necrotic tissue but identified new vocal cord paralysis, for which the patient underwent an elective tracheostomy and placement of a gastrostomy tube 2 days after his initial surgery. He underwent decannulation 2 months later and was discharged home after a 65-day hospitalization, during which he was treated with liposomal amphotericin B (5 mg/kg intravenously daily for 4 weeks) and then transitioned to oral posaconazole (delayed-release, 300 mg daily). At follow-up 1 week after discharge, he reported no significant concerns other than some difficulty with phonation. He was instructed to continue posaconazole for an additional 3 months.

case_info.explanation: A. Initiate liposomal amphotericin B (5 mg/kg intravenously daily) The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that the nonseptate right-angled hyphae present in the sinus mucosal biopsy sample are diagnostic of mucormycosis. Obtaining a serum (1,3)-β-D-glucan level (choice B) would not be helpful because it detects a fungal cell wall component that is absent in mucormycetes. Fluconazole (choice C) is not recommended because it is inactive against fungi that cause mucormycosis. Steroids (choice D) are contraindicated because they may increase the invasiveness of nasopharyngeal mucormycosis. Mucormycosis is a disease caused by a heterogeneous group of more than 250 fungal species.Rhizopus,Mucor,Lichtheimia, andRhizomucorare the most frequent human pathogens1and are present worldwide.2Rhino-orbital-cerebral infection is the most common clinical presentation of mucormycosis, although other organs such as the lung, intestines, and skin can become infected.2,3Rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis typically enters the body through inhalation of spores that deposit in the nasopharynx or through penetrating trauma.2It is a rapidly progressive infection that can involve the brain and is associated with a mortality rate of 25% to 62%.2-4Patients at highest risk of rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis are those with poorly controlled diabetes, high serum iron levels (eg, hemochromatosis), and prolonged neutropenia or impaired cellular immunity (eg, hematologic malignancies; solid organ or bone marrow transplants).2,3SARS-CoV-2 infection is also associated with rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis, especially among patients treated with steroids who develop hyperglycemia.5National epidemiology studies are lacking, but 1 study estimated the annual incidence of mucormycosis at 3 cases/million individuals in the US.6 Patients with mucormycosis may present with orbital swelling, facial pain, proptosis, cranial nerve palsies, headache, acute vision loss, and, in severe cases, a facial necrotic eschar. Among immunosuppressed patients, the primary differential diagnosis is invasive fungal rhinosinusitis due toAspergillus. The diagnosis of mucormycosis is based on histopathology, which shows characteristic nonseptate right-angled hyphae often appearing in “ribbon formations,”3angioinvasion and infarction of surrounding tissue, and, rarely, fruiting bodies, the morphologically distinctive spore-producing component of the fungus. Staining and culture of tissues containing fungus7can help identify fungal species and identify antimicrobial susceptibility. Polymerase chain reaction testing of tissue specimens may be used to identify the specific fungus when histopathology is consistent with mucormycosis but a fungal culture result is negative.3,8 Patients with rhino-orbital-cerebral disease who have risk factors for mucormycosis (eg, uncontrolled diabetes, immunosuppression) need prompt evaluation and surgical debridement of all infected tissue. First-line treatment for rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis is liposomal amphotericin B, which should be administered promptly after diagnosis is suspected and is typically prescribed for 4 to 6 weeks, although duration of therapy depends on clinical improvement and the level of immunosuppression. Oral isavuconazole and posaconazole are less effective medications but may be used if liposomal amphotericin B is contraindicated; they may be coadministered with liposomal amphotericin B in patients with severe disease or may be prescribed as step-down therapy after improvement with liposomal amphotericin B.3 The patient was treated empirically with intravenous liposomal amphotericin B beginning intraoperatively. One week later, the result of an 18s rRNA gene-based polymerase chain reaction test performed on sinus mucosal biopsy tissue was positive for theRhizopus oryzaecomplex. Repeat fiberoptic laryngoscopy on postoperative day 1 revealed no residual necrotic tissue but identified new vocal cord paralysis, for which the patient underwent an elective tracheostomy and placement of a gastrostomy tube 2 days after his initial surgery. He underwent decannulation 2 months later and was discharged home after a 65-day hospitalization, during which he was treated with liposomal amphotericin B (5 mg/kg intravenously daily for 4 weeks) and then transitioned to oral posaconazole (delayed-release, 300 mg daily). At follow-up 1 week after discharge, he reported no significant concerns other than some difficulty with phonation. He was instructed to continue posaconazole for an additional 3 months.

You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

His voice was muffled and his speech was dysarthric. He appeared lethargic but had no focal neurologic deficits. Physical examination findings were normal except for tonsillar edema. White blood cell count was 13.4 ×103/μL (reference, 4-11 ×103/μL); blood glucose level, 274 mg/dL (15.21 mmol/L) (reference, 70-100 mg/dL [3.89-5.55 mmol/L]); serum creatinine level, 0.9 mg/dL (79.56 μmol/L) (reference, 0.4-1.3 mg/dL [35.36-114.92 μmol/L]); bicarbonate level, 9 mmol/L (reference, 20-30 mmol/L); arterial pH, 7.21 (reference, 7.35-7.45); β-hydroxybutyric acid level, 58.2 mg/dL (5590 μmol/L) (reference, <2.81 mg/dL [269.9 μmol/L]); and serum anion gap, 21 (reference, 7-17).    Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.

   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.

   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and

       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.

       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."

   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis

   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: A. Initiate liposomal amphotericin B (5 mg/kg intravenously daily) The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that the nonseptate right-angled hyphae present in the sinus mucosal biopsy sample are diagnostic of mucormycosis. Obtaining a serum (1,3)-β-D-glucan level (choice B) would not be helpful because it detects a fungal cell wall component that is absent in mucormycetes. Fluconazole (choice C) is not recommended because it is inactive against fungi that cause mucormycosis. Steroids (choice D) are contraindicated because they may increase the invasiveness of nasopharyngeal mucormycosis. Mucormycosis is a disease caused by a heterogeneous group of more than 250 fungal species.Rhizopus,Mucor,Lichtheimia, andRhizomucorare the most frequent human pathogens1and are present worldwide.2Rhino-orbital-cerebral infection is the most common clinical presentation of mucormycosis, although other organs such as the lung, intestines, and skin can become infected.2,3Rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis typically enters the body through inhalation of spores that deposit in the nasopharynx or through penetrating trauma.2It is a rapidly progressive infection that can involve the brain and is associated with a mortality rate of 25% to 62%.2-4Patients at highest risk of rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis are those with poorly controlled diabetes, high serum iron levels (eg, hemochromatosis), and prolonged neutropenia or impaired cellular immunity (eg, hematologic malignancies; solid organ or bone marrow transplants).2,3SARS-CoV-2 infection is also associated with rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis, especially among patients treated with steroids who develop hyperglycemia.5National epidemiology studies are lacking, but 1 study estimated the annual incidence of mucormycosis at 3 cases/million individuals in the US.6 Patients with mucormycosis may present with orbital swelling, facial pain, proptosis, cranial nerve palsies, headache, acute vision loss, and, in severe cases, a facial necrotic eschar. Among immunosuppressed patients, the primary differential diagnosis is invasive fungal rhinosinusitis due toAspergillus. The diagnosis of mucormycosis is based on histopathology, which shows characteristic nonseptate right-angled hyphae often appearing in “ribbon formations,”3angioinvasion and infarction of surrounding tissue, and, rarely, fruiting bodies, the morphologically distinctive spore-producing component of the fungus. Staining and culture of tissues containing fungus7can help identify fungal species and identify antimicrobial susceptibility. Polymerase chain reaction testing of tissue specimens may be used to identify the specific fungus when histopathology is consistent with mucormycosis but a fungal culture result is negative.3,8 Patients with rhino-orbital-cerebral disease who have risk factors for mucormycosis (eg, uncontrolled diabetes, immunosuppression) need prompt evaluation and surgical debridement of all infected tissue. First-line treatment for rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis is liposomal amphotericin B, which should be administered promptly after diagnosis is suspected and is typically prescribed for 4 to 6 weeks, although duration of therapy depends on clinical improvement and the level of immunosuppression. Oral isavuconazole and posaconazole are less effective medications but may be used if liposomal amphotericin B is contraindicated; they may be coadministered with liposomal amphotericin B in patients with severe disease or may be prescribed as step-down therapy after improvement with liposomal amphotericin B.3 The patient was treated empirically with intravenous liposomal amphotericin B beginning intraoperatively. One week later, the result of an 18s rRNA gene-based polymerase chain reaction test performed on sinus mucosal biopsy tissue was positive for theRhizopus oryzaecomplex. Repeat fiberoptic laryngoscopy on postoperative day 1 revealed no residual necrotic tissue but identified new vocal cord paralysis, for which the patient underwent an elective tracheostomy and placement of a gastrostomy tube 2 days after his initial surgery. He underwent decannulation 2 months later and was discharged home after a 65-day hospitalization, during which he was treated with liposomal amphotericin B (5 mg/kg intravenously daily for 4 weeks) and then transitioned to oral posaconazole (delayed-release, 300 mg daily). At follow-up 1 week after discharge, he reported no significant concerns other than some difficulty with phonation. He was instructed to continue posaconazole for an additional 3 months.

case_info.explanation: A. Initiate liposomal amphotericin B (5 mg/kg intravenously daily) The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that the nonseptate right-angled hyphae present in the sinus mucosal biopsy sample are diagnostic of mucormycosis. Obtaining a serum (1,3)-β-D-glucan level (choice B) would not be helpful because it detects a fungal cell wall component that is absent in mucormycetes. Fluconazole (choice C) is not recommended because it is inactive against fungi that cause mucormycosis. Steroids (choice D) are contraindicated because they may increase the invasiveness of nasopharyngeal mucormycosis. Mucormycosis is a disease caused by a heterogeneous group of more than 250 fungal species.Rhizopus,Mucor,Lichtheimia, andRhizomucorare the most frequent human pathogens1and are present worldwide.2Rhino-orbital-cerebral infection is the most common clinical presentation of mucormycosis, although other organs such as the lung, intestines, and skin can become infected.2,3Rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis typically enters the body through inhalation of spores that deposit in the nasopharynx or through penetrating trauma.2It is a rapidly progressive infection that can involve the brain and is associated with a mortality rate of 25% to 62%.2-4Patients at highest risk of rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis are those with poorly controlled diabetes, high serum iron levels (eg, hemochromatosis), and prolonged neutropenia or impaired cellular immunity (eg, hematologic malignancies; solid organ or bone marrow transplants).2,3SARS-CoV-2 infection is also associated with rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis, especially among patients treated with steroids who develop hyperglycemia.5National epidemiology studies are lacking, but 1 study estimated the annual incidence of mucormycosis at 3 cases/million individuals in the US.6 Patients with mucormycosis may present with orbital swelling, facial pain, proptosis, cranial nerve palsies, headache, acute vision loss, and, in severe cases, a facial necrotic eschar. Among immunosuppressed patients, the primary differential diagnosis is invasive fungal rhinosinusitis due toAspergillus. The diagnosis of mucormycosis is based on histopathology, which shows characteristic nonseptate right-angled hyphae often appearing in “ribbon formations,”3angioinvasion and infarction of surrounding tissue, and, rarely, fruiting bodies, the morphologically distinctive spore-producing component of the fungus. Staining and culture of tissues containing fungus7can help identify fungal species and identify antimicrobial susceptibility. Polymerase chain reaction testing of tissue specimens may be used to identify the specific fungus when histopathology is consistent with mucormycosis but a fungal culture result is negative.3,8 Patients with rhino-orbital-cerebral disease who have risk factors for mucormycosis (eg, uncontrolled diabetes, immunosuppression) need prompt evaluation and surgical debridement of all infected tissue. First-line treatment for rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis is liposomal amphotericin B, which should be administered promptly after diagnosis is suspected and is typically prescribed for 4 to 6 weeks, although duration of therapy depends on clinical improvement and the level of immunosuppression. Oral isavuconazole and posaconazole are less effective medications but may be used if liposomal amphotericin B is contraindicated; they may be coadministered with liposomal amphotericin B in patients with severe disease or may be prescribed as step-down therapy after improvement with liposomal amphotericin B.3 The patient was treated empirically with intravenous liposomal amphotericin B beginning intraoperatively. One week later, the result of an 18s rRNA gene-based polymerase chain reaction test performed on sinus mucosal biopsy tissue was positive for theRhizopus oryzaecomplex. Repeat fiberoptic laryngoscopy on postoperative day 1 revealed no residual necrotic tissue but identified new vocal cord paralysis, for which the patient underwent an elective tracheostomy and placement of a gastrostomy tube 2 days after his initial surgery. He underwent decannulation 2 months later and was discharged home after a 65-day hospitalization, during which he was treated with liposomal amphotericin B (5 mg/kg intravenously daily for 4 weeks) and then transitioned to oral posaconazole (delayed-release, 300 mg daily). At follow-up 1 week after discharge, he reported no significant concerns other than some difficulty with phonation. He was instructed to continue posaconazole for an additional 3 months.

case_info.explanation: A. Initiate liposomal amphotericin B (5 mg/kg intravenously daily) The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that the nonseptate right-angled hyphae present in the sinus mucosal biopsy sample are diagnostic of mucormycosis. Obtaining a serum (1,3)-β-D-glucan level (choice B) would not be helpful because it detects a fungal cell wall component that is absent in mucormycetes. Fluconazole (choice C) is not recommended because it is inactive against fungi that cause mucormycosis. Steroids (choice D) are contraindicated because they may increase the invasiveness of nasopharyngeal mucormycosis. Mucormycosis is a disease caused by a heterogeneous group of more than 250 fungal species.Rhizopus,Mucor,Lichtheimia, andRhizomucorare the most frequent human pathogens1and are present worldwide.2Rhino-orbital-cerebral infection is the most common clinical presentation of mucormycosis, although other organs such as the lung, intestines, and skin can become infected.2,3Rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis typically enters the body through inhalation of spores that deposit in the nasopharynx or through penetrating trauma.2It is a rapidly progressive infection that can involve the brain and is associated with a mortality rate of 25% to 62%.2-4Patients at highest risk of rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis are those with poorly controlled diabetes, high serum iron levels (eg, hemochromatosis), and prolonged neutropenia or impaired cellular immunity (eg, hematologic malignancies; solid organ or bone marrow transplants).2,3SARS-CoV-2 infection is also associated with rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis, especially among patients treated with steroids who develop hyperglycemia.5National epidemiology studies are lacking, but 1 study estimated the annual incidence of mucormycosis at 3 cases/million individuals in the US.6 Patients with mucormycosis may present with orbital swelling, facial pain, proptosis, cranial nerve palsies, headache, acute vision loss, and, in severe cases, a facial necrotic eschar. Among immunosuppressed patients, the primary differential diagnosis is invasive fungal rhinosinusitis due toAspergillus. The diagnosis of mucormycosis is based on histopathology, which shows characteristic nonseptate right-angled hyphae often appearing in “ribbon formations,”3angioinvasion and infarction of surrounding tissue, and, rarely, fruiting bodies, the morphologically distinctive spore-producing component of the fungus. Staining and culture of tissues containing fungus7can help identify fungal species and identify antimicrobial susceptibility. Polymerase chain reaction testing of tissue specimens may be used to identify the specific fungus when histopathology is consistent with mucormycosis but a fungal culture result is negative.3,8 Patients with rhino-orbital-cerebral disease who have risk factors for mucormycosis (eg, uncontrolled diabetes, immunosuppression) need prompt evaluation and surgical debridement of all infected tissue. First-line treatment for rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis is liposomal amphotericin B, which should be administered promptly after diagnosis is suspected and is typically prescribed for 4 to 6 weeks, although duration of therapy depends on clinical improvement and the level of immunosuppression. Oral isavuconazole and posaconazole are less effective medications but may be used if liposomal amphotericin B is contraindicated; they may be coadministered with liposomal amphotericin B in patients with severe disease or may be prescribed as step-down therapy after improvement with liposomal amphotericin B.3 The patient was treated empirically with intravenous liposomal amphotericin B beginning intraoperatively. One week later, the result of an 18s rRNA gene-based polymerase chain reaction test performed on sinus mucosal biopsy tissue was positive for theRhizopus oryzaecomplex. Repeat fiberoptic laryngoscopy on postoperative day 1 revealed no residual necrotic tissue but identified new vocal cord paralysis, for which the patient underwent an elective tracheostomy and placement of a gastrostomy tube 2 days after his initial surgery. He underwent decannulation 2 months later and was discharged home after a 65-day hospitalization, during which he was treated with liposomal amphotericin B (5 mg/kg intravenously daily for 4 weeks) and then transitioned to oral posaconazole (delayed-release, 300 mg daily). At follow-up 1 week after discharge, he reported no significant concerns other than some difficulty with phonation. He was instructed to continue posaconazole for an additional 3 months.

case_info.explanation: A. Initiate liposomal amphotericin B (5 mg/kg intravenously daily) The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that the nonseptate right-angled hyphae present in the sinus mucosal biopsy sample are diagnostic of mucormycosis. Obtaining a serum (1,3)-β-D-glucan level (choice B) would not be helpful because it detects a fungal cell wall component that is absent in mucormycetes. Fluconazole (choice C) is not recommended because it is inactive against fungi that cause mucormycosis. Steroids (choice D) are contraindicated because they may increase the invasiveness of nasopharyngeal mucormycosis. Mucormycosis is a disease caused by a heterogeneous group of more than 250 fungal species.Rhizopus,Mucor,Lichtheimia, andRhizomucorare the most frequent human pathogens1and are present worldwide.2Rhino-orbital-cerebral infection is the most common clinical presentation of mucormycosis, although other organs such as the lung, intestines, and skin can become infected.2,3Rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis typically enters the body through inhalation of spores that deposit in the nasopharynx or through penetrating trauma.2It is a rapidly progressive infection that can involve the brain and is associated with a mortality rate of 25% to 62%.2-4Patients at highest risk of rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis are those with poorly controlled diabetes, high serum iron levels (eg, hemochromatosis), and prolonged neutropenia or impaired cellular immunity (eg, hematologic malignancies; solid organ or bone marrow transplants).2,3SARS-CoV-2 infection is also associated with rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis, especially among patients treated with steroids who develop hyperglycemia.5National epidemiology studies are lacking, but 1 study estimated the annual incidence of mucormycosis at 3 cases/million individuals in the US.6 Patients with mucormycosis may present with orbital swelling, facial pain, proptosis, cranial nerve palsies, headache, acute vision loss, and, in severe cases, a facial necrotic eschar. Among immunosuppressed patients, the primary differential diagnosis is invasive fungal rhinosinusitis due toAspergillus. The diagnosis of mucormycosis is based on histopathology, which shows characteristic nonseptate right-angled hyphae often appearing in “ribbon formations,”3angioinvasion and infarction of surrounding tissue, and, rarely, fruiting bodies, the morphologically distinctive spore-producing component of the fungus. Staining and culture of tissues containing fungus7can help identify fungal species and identify antimicrobial susceptibility. Polymerase chain reaction testing of tissue specimens may be used to identify the specific fungus when histopathology is consistent with mucormycosis but a fungal culture result is negative.3,8 Patients with rhino-orbital-cerebral disease who have risk factors for mucormycosis (eg, uncontrolled diabetes, immunosuppression) need prompt evaluation and surgical debridement of all infected tissue. First-line treatment for rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis is liposomal amphotericin B, which should be administered promptly after diagnosis is suspected and is typically prescribed for 4 to 6 weeks, although duration of therapy depends on clinical improvement and the level of immunosuppression. Oral isavuconazole and posaconazole are less effective medications but may be used if liposomal amphotericin B is contraindicated; they may be coadministered with liposomal amphotericin B in patients with severe disease or may be prescribed as step-down therapy after improvement with liposomal amphotericin B.3 The patient was treated empirically with intravenous liposomal amphotericin B beginning intraoperatively. One week later, the result of an 18s rRNA gene-based polymerase chain reaction test performed on sinus mucosal biopsy tissue was positive for theRhizopus oryzaecomplex. Repeat fiberoptic laryngoscopy on postoperative day 1 revealed no residual necrotic tissue but identified new vocal cord paralysis, for which the patient underwent an elective tracheostomy and placement of a gastrostomy tube 2 days after his initial surgery. He underwent decannulation 2 months later and was discharged home after a 65-day hospitalization, during which he was treated with liposomal amphotericin B (5 mg/kg intravenously daily for 4 weeks) and then transitioned to oral posaconazole (delayed-release, 300 mg daily). At follow-up 1 week after discharge, he reported no significant concerns other than some difficulty with phonation. He was instructed to continue posaconazole for an additional 3 months.

[Case]
A 41-year-old man with type 1 diabetes and a hemoglobin A1clevel of 16.8% (reference, 4.0%-5.6%) 1 month prior to admission presented to the emergency department with 1 week of generalized weakness. His temperature was 38.5 °C (101.3 °F); blood pressure, 125/75 mm Hg; heart rate, 95/min; respiratory rate, 24/min; and oxygen saturation, 96% on room air. His voice was muffled and his speech was dysarthric. He appeared lethargic but had no focal neurologic deficits. Physical examination findings were normal except for tonsillar edema. White blood cell count was 13.4 ×103/μL (reference, 4-11 ×103/μL); blood glucose level, 274 mg/dL (15.21 mmol/L) (reference, 70-100 mg/dL [3.89-5.55 mmol/L]); serum creatinine level, 0.9 mg/dL (79.56 μmol/L) (reference, 0.4-1.3 mg/dL [35.36-114.92 μmol/L]); bicarbonate level, 9 mmol/L (reference, 20-30 mmol/L); arterial pH, 7.21 (reference, 7.35-7.45); β-hydroxybutyric acid level, 58.2 mg/dL (5590 μmol/L) (reference, <2.81 mg/dL [269.9 μmol/L]); and serum anion gap, 21 (reference, 7-17). Findings on a chest radiograph were normal. A computed tomography scan of the head and neck with intravenous contrast showed mucosal thickening of the maxillary and ethmoid sinuses, and prominence of the adenoids and palatine tonsils. Flexible laryngoscopy showed patent nasal sinuses and mucosal edema without abscess or necrosis. He was treated with intravenous fluids and with insulin, vancomycin (1 g intravenously every 12 hours), and piperacillin-tazobactam (4.5 g intravenously every 6 hours). On hospital day 2, his temperature was 38.9 °C (102 °F). A repeat computed tomography scan of the neck demonstrated soft-tissue gas in the nasopharynx and prevertebral fascia (Figure, left panel). Flexible laryngoscopy revealed necrotic tissue throughout the nasopharynx. Emergent transnasal endoscopic debridement of the maxillary, sphenoid, and ethmoid sinuses was performed. Sinus mucosal samples grewCandida albicansin fungal cultures, and histopathology identified numerous broad, nonseptate right-angled hyphae and fruiting bodies (Figure, right panel).
